extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and newspaper journalists covering court cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on gathering, shaping, and writing news about criminal and civil court proceedings so stories are accurate, legally responsible, and interesting to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational or destructive treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Destructive, or anti-social, influences ... are found in those court stories — particularly those of criminal and divorce cases — that play up disgusting or scandalous phases of such trials in order to gratify the morbid taste of some of their readers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emphasize disgusting or scandalous details merely to gratify morbid curiosity. Be aware that criminal and divorce cases are especially prone to such treatment. Favor constructive stories of crime that serve the public interest rather than exploiting lurid aspects for readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'try the case' in the newspaper / avoid prejudicial pretrial publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some newspapers undertake to prove the innocence or the guilt of an accused person by printing whatever evidence they can secure, even though some of it would be excluded from the trial under the rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from publishing evidence or editorial conclusions that could create public opinion or arouse feeling sufficient to prevent the accused from having a fair trial. Avoid presenting material that would be inadmissible in court as though it were definitive. Recognize the ethical and legal danger in 'trying the case in the newspaper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and present matters of general significance clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: To find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, and to present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy, are the main problems in handling court news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should dig through legal language to surface what matters to general readers, explain technical points plainly, and make the story engaging while maintaining factual and legal accuracy. Balancing clarity/attractiveness with accuracy is the central task of court reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical body composition of a court news story
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of court news stories usually consists of summaries of arguments, decisions, testimony, or legal documents, or of excerpts from them, with the necessary connective material. In some instances the story is largely a history of the case or action and of the persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summaries and carefully chosen excerpts (with connective context) to convey the essential legal proceedings. When appropriate, provide background/history of the case and person profiles to help readers understand significance. Ensure connective material explains why quoted/excerpted items matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead selection — let the status of the case determine the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is usually determined by the status of the case. Any one of the important points may be made the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the lead based on what is currently most newsworthy (verdict, sentencing, key testimony, pleading, procedural development). Be flexible: different stories on the same case can feature different primary points depending on timing and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms for presenting testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in news stories is given in one of three forms: (1) the question indicated by "Q" and the answer by "A," both question and answer given in one paragraph without quotation marks, (2) the question and the answer in quotation marks, each followed by the necessary explanatory matter and each in a separate paragraph, like verbatim conversation in fiction, (3) a summary of the testimony of each witness in indirect quotation form, with the name of the witness at or near the beginning of the first sentence of the summarized testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one of the three clear formats consistently so readers can follow courtroom exchanges. Q/A format (with or without quotation marks) conveys verbatim exchanges; indirect summary is suitable for compressing testimony or when verbatim wording is unnecessary. Place the witness's name prominently when summarizing to maintain clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential details to include in a court story
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details, however, are (1) the verdict and the conditions under which it was rendered, (2) the sentence imposed, (3) the decision rendered and its significance, (4) important testimony, (5) net results of the day's proceedings in a trial, (6) the history of the case or action, (7) provisions of a will, (8) liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy, (9) the award, or finding, (10) the grounds on which a suit is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the story covers the specific elements relevant to the case type (criminal, civil, probate, bankruptcy, etc.). Explain context (conditions, significance, grounds) so readers understand consequences. Tailor which of these elements to emphasize based on the lead and the case's current status.
